## 1 Abstract

A Divisia aggregate depends on two choices besides the data: the
benchmark rate that prices the user costs, and the index formula. This
vignette shows on the simulated data `money_sim` how much each matters,
and when the Divisia aggregate and the simple sum part ways.

## 2 The benchmark rate

``` r

data(money_sim)
bench <- list(
    `largest component rate` = NULL
  , `bond yield (rb)`        = "rb"
  , `bond yield + 1 point`   = money_sim$rb + 1
  , `bond yield + 3 points`  = money_sim$rb + 3
  )
growth <-
  vapply(
      X         = bench
    , FUN       = function(b) {
        d <-
          dmai(
              .data     = money_sim
            , method    = "Barnett"
            , logbase   = NULL
            , date      = "Date"
            , x         = NULL
            , r         = NULL
            , user_cost = NULL
            , benchmark = b
            , percent   = TRUE
            , base      = 100
            , as_dt     = TRUE
            )
        100 * ((d$index[nrow(d)] / d$index[1L])^(12 / (nrow(d) - 1)) - 1)
      }
    , FUN.VALUE = numeric(length = 1)
    )
round(x = growth, digits = 2)
```

    largest component rate        bond yield (rb)   bond yield + 1 point
                     10.21                  11.27                  11.50
     bond yield + 3 points
                     11.81 

With the largest component rate as the benchmark the aggregate grows
10.2% a year, against 11.3% with the bond yield. The component with the
largest rate, the time deposits over one year, then has a user cost of
zero at most dates and almost no weight, although it grows fastest. A
benchmark above every component rate gives every component some weight;
raising it further raises the weights of the interest-bearing deposits
(their user costs rise proportionally more than that of currency), so
the aggregate moves towards the simple sum.

``` r

w <- function(b) {
  u <-
    dmai_user_cost(
        .data     = money_sim
      , date      = "Date"
      , x         = NULL
      , r         = NULL
      , benchmark = b
      , percent   = TRUE
      )$components
  u[, .(share = mean(share)), by = component]
}
merge(w(NULL), w("rb"), by = "component", suffixes = c("_largest_rate", "_bond_yield"))
```

## 3 The index formula

``` r

cmp <-
  dmai_compare(
      .data     = money_sim
    , methods   = c("Barnett", "Hancock", "Fisher", "SimpleSum", "CE")
    , logbase   = NULL
    , date      = "Date"
    , x         = NULL
    , r         = NULL
    , user_cost = NULL
    , benchmark = "rb"
    , percent   = TRUE
    , base      = 100
    )
cmp$summary
```

          method mean_growth annual_growth sd_growth last_index
          <fctr>       <num>         <num>     <num>      <num>
    1:   Barnett   0.8896048      11.26589 0.5902133   838.2578
    2:   Hancock   0.9043824      11.38584 0.5953797   856.4399
    3:    Fisher   0.8895995      11.26582 0.5902227   838.2471
    4: SimpleSum   1.0055352      12.82460 0.5725592  1105.8829
    5:        CE   0.8347407      10.53576 2.6929846   735.2426

``` r

plot(
    x     = cmp
  , which = "growth"
  )
```

![](data:image/webp;base64,)

Divisia and Fisher differ by less than a thousandth of the index; the
choice between superlative formulas hardly matters. The simple-sum
aggregate grows about one and a half points a year faster. The currency
equivalent index moves with the level of the rates: when the benchmark
falls, the deposits count as more money-like and the index jumps.

## 4 When the simple sum misleads

The gap between the growth of the simple sum and of the Divisia
aggregate comes from the components that grow faster or slower than the
others. The Divisia second moment measures that spread:

``` r

fit <-
  dmai(
      .data     = money_sim
    , method    = c("Barnett", "Hancock", "Fisher", "SimpleSum", "CE")
    , logbase   = NULL
    , date      = "Date"
    , x         = NULL
    , r         = NULL
    , user_cost = NULL
    , benchmark = "rb"
    , percent   = TRUE
    , base      = 100
    , as_dt     = FALSE
    )
gap <- fit$simple_sum$growth - fit$index$DMAI
sd  <-
  dmai_moments(
      .data = fit
    )$moments$sd
cor(x = abs(gap), y = sd, use = "complete.obs")
```

    [1] 0.3556961

``` r

d <- data.table::data.table(Date = fit$index$Date, gap = gap, sd = sd)[!is.na(gap)]
ggplot2::ggplot(data = d, mapping = ggplot2::aes(x = sd, y = abs(gap))) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(colour = "#1f4e9e", alpha = 0.6) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Divisia standard deviation of component growth (percent)",
                y = "|simple sum - Divisia growth| (points)") +
  dmai_theme(
      base_size       = 11
    , base_family     = "serif"
    , ticks_inward    = TRUE
    , legend_position = "bottom"
    )
```

![](data:image/webp;base64,)

The correlation is 0.36: months with a larger spread of component growth
tend to be months in which the two aggregates disagree more, the
diagnostic of Barnett and Serletis (1990). In these simulated data much
of the gap is the steady trend difference between the components, which
the spread of a single month does not capture.

## 5 References

Barnett, W. A. (1980). Economic monetary aggregates: an application of
index number and aggregation theory. *Journal of Econometrics*, 14(1),
11–48.

Barnett, W. A. and Serletis, A. (1990). A dispersion-dependency
diagnostic test for aggregation error: with applications to monetary
economics and income distribution. *Journal of Econometrics*, 43(1–2),
5–34.

Rotemberg, J. J., Driscoll, J. C. and Poterba, J. M. (1995). Money,
output, and prices: evidence from a new monetary aggregate. *Journal of
Business and Economic Statistics*, 13(1), 67–83.
